stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 4.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 302 K and 1.03 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 32.0 mL of 0.13 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.11 M NaOH.
9.8 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 51 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 3.6 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Na (Z = 11) and Mg (Z = 12) are compared.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 179 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 44.09 g/mol.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.002 M solution of $$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.002 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 29 g. The actual yield is 20 g. What is the percent yield?
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 26 g. The actual yield is 16.1 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of $$\ce{Ba(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.1 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.8 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.5 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.7 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of arsenic (As, Z = 33)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 33 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: Which substance is most soluble in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?

options.why: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, Cl2 70.9, He 4, Ar 40.

questions.stem: The nitrate ion has three resonance structures. What is true of its N–O bonds?

options.text: One is double and two are single at all times
They alternate rapidly between single and double
All three are identical, intermediate between single and double bonds

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of C in $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 3 atoms of C in the formula.

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

options.text: F is less electronegative than I

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: A 30.7 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 19.7 mL of 0.194 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 3. A mixture has [A] = 0.9 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.2 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.317
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.0635
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.0635
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.0635, which is less than K.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{BaSO4}$$ is 1.1 \times 10^{-10}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

options.why: This salt gives two ions: Ksp = s².

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 23 L flask at 0.553 atm and 282 K?
A solution has an absorbance of 1.22 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 380 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the oxidation number of N in $$\ce{NO3^-}$$?

options.why: Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 17. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: 31 g of water at 63 °C is mixed with 51 g of water at 29 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.4 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.26 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 3.2. A mixture has [A] = 0.4 M, [B] = 0.5 M and [C] = 0.9 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 4.05
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 4.05, which is greater than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 4.05
options.why: If Q is greater than K, the reaction proceeds in reverse.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 4.5

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 39 kJ/mol, the transition state at 134 kJ/mol and the products at 7 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 95, ΔH = -32, reverse Ea = 127 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.346 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{H2O}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{BaO}$$ or $$\ce{MgF2}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{BaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

questions.explanation: BaO has ion charges 2 and 2; MgF2 has 2 and 1.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{CH2O}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.
Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel

questions.explanation: CH2O is trigonal planar; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.7 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.083 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 208 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 7.1 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 6170 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of bromine shows two peaks: mass 79 with relative abundance 46% and mass 81 with 54%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.

questions.stem: At equilibrium, which statement is true?

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal
options.why: They are constant, not necessarily equal.

options.text: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 627 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 10.9. In a solution at pH 9.9, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.179 mol of solute in enough water to make 211 mL of solution?
What volume does 2.56 mol of gas occupy at 1.78 atm and 262 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -380 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -201 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: A compound (ethane) is 79.9% C, 20.1% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to CH3; the molecular formula is C2H6.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 697, 1255, 1770, 14160 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 3 electrons, so it has 3 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = -77 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 153 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 798 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.5 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.48 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 6.35) and 0.32 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
A buffer contains 0.21 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.06 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 4.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×4, so order 2 in B.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.87) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 34.8 mL. What is the pH after 17.4 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2CO + O2 -> 2CO2}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.
Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 6 electrons transferred and E° = 1.22 V.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 11 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -4.44; K = 0.0118. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$, 16 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$ reacts with 66 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. C3H8 is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 35 min. Starting at 14.5 M, what is the concentration after 175 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Mg.
Explain why the 1s peak of Mg has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Na.

rubric.criterion: Mg has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Mg has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Na: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
